Southern Africa. The southernmost subregion of the African continent, encompassing South Africa, Namibia, Botswana, Zimbabwe, Lesotho, Eswatini, and surrounding territories, characterized by the Kalahari Desert, vast mineral wealth, and a history of colonialism, racial segregation, and dramatic political transformation. The region's 21st-century trajectory has been shaped by the legacies of European settlement and apartheid.

South Africa, the region's largest and most developed country, was colonized by the Dutch in the 17th century and then by the British, leading to a settler-colonial society dominated by European minorities over African majorities. The Kalahari Desert occupies much of Botswana and Namibia, creating arid landscapes inhabited by the San people. It is one of Africa's largest deserts and shaped human settlement patterns historically.

Apartheid from 1948 to 1994 was South Africa's systematic racial-segregation regime, enforcing racial hierarchy through law and violence. It provoked international isolation, internal resistance, and became a symbol of racism to the world. Nelson Mandela, a resistance leader imprisoned for 27 years, emerged as the face of anti-apartheid struggle. His release and election as president in 1994 marked the transition to majority-rule democracy and became an international symbol of reconciliation.

The region is rich in minerals. South Africa dominates gold and diamonds. Namibia and Botswana contain rich diamond deposits. This wealth attracted colonial exploitation and later drove geopolitics. The Zambezi River forms borders between countries and powered major infrastructure projects like the Kariba Dam. It is central to the region's ecology and hydroelectric power.

Post-apartheid Southern Africa has experienced economic inequality, political instability in some countries such as Zimbabwe under Mugabe, and continued social challenges. South Africa remains the region's economic powerhouse but faces inequality and corruption.
